title: What does challenging the frame cost?
author: Luca Foppoli
summary: Luca Foppoli continues his series on whether corporate professionals ever chose their careers or only their next job, asking what it costs to question the frame itself. He names two costs. The first is identity: a confident job-title answer to what do you do gives you a place in the world, while an honest but fluid answer sounds lost. The second is the past, because questioning the structure of your life invites doubt about every choice that led to it. He argues the costs are worth paying, since the alternative is reaching the end of life having borrowed an identity from a structure you never examined. He then shows that every outcome of the questioning is acceptable: you may keep your job knowing it is truly yours, take a better next step, or choose a quieter life. Borrowing from Nietzsche, he suggests that accepting the past turns every it was into a thus I willed it, and he reports that after sleepless nights he chose to stay for now, knowing why.
points: Foppoli names identity as the first cost: a crisp corporate title feels solid, while an honest answer about a changing portfolio of work can feel like being lost.
The second cost is the past, because questioning your current frame forces you to ask whether the chain of earlier choices was a mistake.
His argument for paying the cost is the fear of reaching the end and realising you borrowed your identity from a structure you accepted as true.
Every result of the questioning is acceptable, including deciding to keep your job, so the point is ownership of the choice rather than a particular outcome.
Accepting the past, in his Nietzschean phrase, turns what happened to you into a road you willed.
quotes: Challenging the frame means challenging the identity you have been using for years. Good luck.

Neither version explains what you actually do, but the first sounds more serious and grounded in reality. You look in the mirror, say the first and it feels like you own a specific place in the world.
Questioning your current frame inevitably leads to questioning the choices that brought you there. Ouch.
There is nothing I fear more than reaching the end, looking back and realizing I never chose my identity, but rather I borrowed it from a structure I accepted as true.
What if you do the questioning and then choose to keep your job and your life as they are? Fantastic, I’m happy for you. It means that what happened to you was in line with what you wanted all along.

It is only by accepting your past that you can turn it into the road that led you to where you are, rather than something that happened to you. Stealing from Nietzsche: you turn every “it was” into a “thus I willed it”.
